<a id="s0"></a>
## 0. Intro

- First of a series of system design breakdowns
- Question: design a ticket booking service like Ticketmaster
  - Asked a lot at Meta, especially in the "product design" interview
  - Also asked often in the regular system design interview
- Speaker background
  - 5 years at Meta as an interviewer and staff engineer
  - Co-founder of Hello Interview (mocks with senior FAANG engineers and managers)
  - Has asked this question well over 50 times, at Meta and in mocks
  - Has seen where candidates of all levels do well and trip up
- Format
  - Walk through as a real interview
  - Interject with tips, frameworks, lessons learned from mocks
- A written breakdown also exists on hellointerview.com

<a id="s1"></a>
## 1. The Roadmap

- Suggested for any SD interview, especially user-facing products
- Steps
  1. Requirements
     - Functional: the features of the system
     - Non-functional: the qualities of the system
  2. Core entities
     - The data persisted and exchanged through the system
  3. API
  4. High-level design
     - A simple design that satisfies the functional requirements
  5. Deep dives
     - A conversation with the interviewer
     - Depending on level, the interviewer might lead it
     - Goes deeper, mainly into satisfying the non-functional requirements

<a id="s2"></a>
## 2. Functional Requirements

- Write these down first
  - Statements like "users should be able to…"
- If you haven't used the system, ask the interviewer a lot
  - What is it for, most important functionality, features, how users use it
- Then list the core features
  - Core = most necessary to make the system work
- Walk backwards through the user flow
  1. Users should be able to **book tickets** (most important)
  2. To book, a user must **view an event**
     - Event page, seat map, choose a seat
     - Event details: who's performing, etc.
  3. To get to an event, users need discovery: **search for events**
- The user flow
  - Search, see a drop-down list of events
  - Click one, go to the event page
  - Book a ticket from there
- These are what most candidates land on
  - Also what the speaker pushes candidates toward if they need help

<a id="s3"></a>
## 3. Non-Functional Requirements

<a id="s3-1"></a>
### 3.1 The Biggest Mistake

- NFRs are qualities, not features
  - Scalability, availability, reliability, fault tolerance…
- Mistake: just writing those terms down
  - Not strictly wrong, but defeats the purpose
  - All systems have those qualities
- The point: identify what makes **this** system unique, interesting, challenging
  - Go through the "-ilities" in the context of this specific problem

<a id="s3-2"></a>
### 3.2 CAP: Consistency vs Availability

- First question to ask: does the system prioritize availability or consistency?
- Easy right answer, especially for mid-level
  - Prioritize consistency over availability
  - Reason: no ticket assigned to more than one user
  - **No double booking**
- More nuanced, senior-level answer
  - The two can coexist, in different parts of the system / architecture
  - **Strong consistency for booking tickets**
  - **High availability for search and viewing events**
- Why
  - Search / view: a newly added event not visible for a couple of seconds is fine
  - Booking: if a user in Germany buys the ticket I'm viewing in America
    - I need to know instantly
    - Or get an error because I can't book it anymore

<a id="s3-3"></a>
### 3.3 Read / Write Ratio

- Reads are much greater than writes
  - Probably ~100:1, maybe even 1000:1
  - ~100:1 if booking conversion rate is ~1%
- Many more people search and view than buy
- This has consequences on the design later

<a id="s3-4"></a>
### 3.4 Query Access Pattern

- How is the site used? Frequency, consistency, irregularity of requests
- People don't book all that much; fairly regular and even
- Until a really popular event
  - Taylor Swift tour, Super Bowl, World Cup
  - Tens, maybe hundreds of millions at the front door for the same tickets
- So: don't just write "scalability"
  - Write: **scalability to handle surges from popular events**

<a id="s3-5"></a>
### 3.5 Below The Line

- Other things matter too
  - Not losing data, GDPR compliance, fault tolerance, etc.
- Note them as "below the line" (out of scope)
- Then check in with the interviewer
  - "These are what I'll prioritize; here's what I consider out of scope"
  - "Would you like me to reprioritize? Move anything up or down?"
- Shows larger product thinking while staying focused on what matters

<a id="s4"></a>
## 4. Core Entities

- Done together with the API; they come hand in hand
  - Usually ≤ ~2 min on entities, up to ~5 min on the API
- Purpose: understand what data is persisted and exchanged by the APIs
  - Used to build the APIs and the high-level design
- Entities
  - **Event**: added by admins (adding events is out of scope; focus on the user flow)
  - **Venue**: where events are hosted, like a stadium
  - **Performer**: who performs
  - **Ticket**: all tickets for an event
    - Whether available, who purchased, price, etc.
- Probably a table / collection for each
- Fields
  - You can list fields now (name, description…)
  - Speaker's advice: stick to entities only
  - Tell the interviewer: "I won't detail fields yet; I'm too early, they'll evolve"
  - Be explicit about fields in the high-level design

<a id="s5"></a>
## 5. API

<a id="s5-1"></a>
### 5.1 Method

- Strictly the user-facing APIs the client calls to satisfy the functional requirements
- Look back at each functional requirement
  - Create one or more APIs for each
  - They take and return entities, or their fields
- REST is typical in these interviews
  - Consider other options; GraphQL is the main other one

<a id="s5-2"></a>
### 5.2 View Event

```
GET /event/:eventId
-> Event & Venue & Performer & Ticket[]
```

- Everything needed to render the event page
- Ticket list is for rendering the seat map
  - Which tickets are available, where the seats are

<a id="s5-3"></a>
### 5.3 Search

```
GET /search?term=&location=&type=&date=...
-> Partial<Event>[]
```

- Term: free text
- Location: maybe lat/long; abstracted for now
- Type / category: sports, music, etc.
- Date ranges: probably really important
- All optional
- "Partial" (TypeScript-inspired pseudo-code)
  - Just enough to show search results: name, description, performer
  - Click a result, then hit the view-event endpoint for full detail

<a id="s5-4"></a>
### 5.4 Booking Is Two-Phase

- Like Ticketmaster or buying an airline ticket
  - See a seat map, choose a seat
  - Then a second phase to purchase, with a countdown (maybe 10 min)
  - During that time the ticket is reserved for you
  - Don't book in time, it goes back to available
- In interviews
  - Some candidates know it's two-phase: awesome to see, not required
  - If a candidate writes one endpoint, the speaker points it out; they amend

```
POST /booking/reserve
header: JWT | sessionToken
body: { ticketId }

PUT /booking/confirm
header: JWT | sessionToken
body: { ticketId, paymentDetails }
```

- Reserve
  - Body is just a ticket ID
  - Variations allow multiple seats; keep it simple: one seat = one ticket
  - Reserves the ticket for 10 minutes; client goes to a payment page
- No user ID in the body, on purpose
  - Security concern: a body can be altered
  - Anyone knowing a user ID could reserve on their behalf
  - User info goes in the header: JWT or session token
  - Nice to note; shows technical excellence; don't spend long on it
- Confirm
  - Ticket ID + payment details
  - Offload payment to Stripe
  - Stripe "payment intents" with client libraries (React or raw JS) collect payment info
  - Posted back to your server
- Method nuance
  - Maybe PUT or PATCH, since not creating a new entry
  - Not the most important thing

<a id="s6"></a>
## 6. High-Level Design

<a id="s6-1"></a>
### 6.1 Setup

- About 15 minutes in at this point
  - Leaves ~20 minutes for HLD and deep dives, give or take by level
- Goal: a simple design that satisfies the three functional requirements
- Components
  - Client
  - Microservices architecture
    - By far the most common setup in these interviews
    - If unsure which architecture, microservices is probably right
  - API Gateway
    - Main job: route incoming requests to the right microservice
    - Also: authentication, often rate limiting
- Method: go one by one through the API requests (which map to FRs)

```
Client -> API Gateway -> Event CRUD Service -> Postgres
                      -> Search Service    -> Postgres
                      -> Booking Service   -> Postgres, Stripe
```

<a id="s6-2"></a>
### 6.2 View Event Flow

- Gateway routes to the **Event CRUD Service**
  - Responsible for create / read / update / delete of events
  - Most CRUD is out of scope; only the view path here
- Service reads from the database
- Tables
  - **Event**: id, venueId (FK), performer / team, name, description, …
    - One-to-many to tickets (foreign keys, not ticket data)
  - **Venue**: id, location, seat map, …
  - **Performer**: id, …
  - **Ticket**: id, seat (the location), price, eventId (relation back)
- Flow
  - Join event + venue + performer, plus available tickets
  - Return to the client

<a id="s6-3"></a>
### 6.3 Database Choice

- Properties that matter
  - Consistency, especially for tickets
  - Decent relationships: one-to-one, one-to-many
- Pick: **Postgres**
  - One the speaker uses frequently
  - ACID on tickets, transactions, good for mild relational queries
- NoSQL would be fine too, e.g., DynamoDB
- SQL vs NoSQL is an old, uninteresting debate
  - What matters: the qualities of the database you need
  - Most things one can do, the other can do nowadays
  - DynamoDB has ACID properties, for example
- Seniority signal
  - Mid-level candidates break down SQL vs NoSQL at length
  - Senior candidates: "here are the qualities I need; either works; I pick Postgres because I know it"
- Now is the time to map fields and columns
  - Put them next to the database; they'll evolve during the design

<a id="s6-4"></a>
### 6.4 Search Flow (Simple First)

- Add a **Search Service**
- As simple as possible: a SQL query
  - `SELECT * FROM db WHERE type IN (...) AND name LIKE '%term%'`
- This "totally sucks" and is incredibly slow
  - Wildcards force a full table scan
- Leave it for now
  - Say in the interview: "this won't cut it; I'll optimize after satisfying all FRs"

<a id="s6-5"></a>
### 6.5 Booking Flow

- Add a **Booking Service**
- Reserve
  - Look up the ticket row by ticket ID
  - New column **status**: available / reserved / booked
  - Set to reserved, return 200
- Confirm
  - Takes ticket ID + payment details
  - Call Stripe, a third-party processor
    - Payments can usually be abstracted away
    - Unless the interview is for a payments team
  - Stripe handles payment asynchronously
    - Reaches out to card companies / bank (happens quickly)
    - Calls back not in the response, but via a **webhook**
    - You register a callback URL; the booking service exposes an endpoint
    - Good to know, maybe not necessary for the interview
  - On success: set ticket status to **booked**, plus the **user ID** who booked
  - Maybe send an email: out of scope

<a id="s6-6"></a>
### 6.6 The Expiry Problem

- What if the 10-minute countdown is exceeded?
  - User closes the laptop, decides not to buy
- Status stays reserved forever
  - Seat map queries "available", so the seat is excluded
  - Seat infinitely reserved: wrong; must expire after 10 minutes

<a id="s6-7"></a>
### 6.7 Option 1: Reserved Timestamp

- Add a **reservedTimestamp** column
- Availability query
  - `status = available OR (status = reserved AND reservedTimestamp < now - 10 min)`
- Works
- Downside
  - Confusing data model
  - Status says reserved while it isn't really
  - Two fields to keep consistent

<a id="s6-8"></a>
### 6.8 Option 2: Cron Job

- Runs every ~10 minutes
- Queries every ticket in reserved status
  - If reservedTimestamp > 10 min ago, set back to available
- Valid approach; **passing for mid-level**
- Not enough for senior, staff, principal
  - Introduces a delta `n` between when it should unreserve and when the cron runs
  - Example: should unreserve at 12:00, cron runs at 12:09
    - `n` = 9 minutes
    - Ticket reserved for 19 minutes, not 10
- Need something more real-time

<a id="s6-9"></a>
### 6.9 Option 3: Distributed Lock With TTL

- Remove the cron job, the reservedTimestamp, and the reserved status
- Add a **distributed lock**: the "ticket lock"
  - Redis, or any in-memory cache
- Reserve
  - Don't write to the database at all
  - Set `ticketId -> true` with **TTL 10 minutes** (value doesn't matter)
  - After 10 minutes the key is deleted immediately
- View event (Event CRUD Service)
  - Query DB for tickets with status available
  - Look each ticket ID up in Redis
  - If locked, remove from the available list
  - Return to the client
- User closed the laptop
  - Key expires at 10 minutes
  - Next seat map query: not in the lock, so shown as available
- Why distributed, not in-memory in the booking service
  - Multiple booking service instances; it scales horizontally
  - All need the same consistent, single view of the lock
- "Sort of the optimal answer"

<a id="s6-10"></a>
### 6.10 What If The Lock Goes Down?

- Detect and immediately bring a new one up
- Users who reserved in the last 10 minutes lose their reservation
  - For a 10-minute window, several users could reach payment for the same ticket
- Consistency is not lost
  - Postgres ACID on the write to available / booked
  - One write completes before another can read
  - Whoever submits purchase first wins; the other gets an error
- Bad UX for users in that window
- A conversation with the product team: is that OK in an unlikely disaster?
- Speaker would argue it's fine

<a id="s6-11"></a>
### 6.11 HLD Status

- Satisfies all functional requirements
- Not perfect: doesn't scale, search is not great
- Handle those in deep dives

<a id="s7"></a>
## 7. Deep Dives

<a id="s7-1"></a>
### 7.1 How To Approach

- Where senior and staff candidates "earn their keep"
- Mid-level
  - The board so far might already pass, especially with the Redis lock
  - Most mid-level candidates land on the cron job
  - Interviewer may ask about scaling, slow search; answer well
- Senior / staff
  - Show depth in **one to three places**
  - Not the only places; not ones the interviewer explicitly looks for
  - Up to you where you lead
- Process: reference the NFRs, see what's missing
- The speaker missed "low latency search" originally
  - Realized it while designing; went back and added it
  - Totally OK; you can and should do that

<a id="s7-2"></a>
### 7.2 Low-Latency Search: Elasticsearch

- Current search is slow: full table scan
- Common solution: a search-optimized database
  - **Elasticsearch**, recommended for interviews
- Inverted index
  - Tokenize event text (name, description…) into terms
  - Example: "the Philadelphia Eagles are playing in a wild card match-up against the Broncos"
    - Terms: Philadelphia, Eagles, playoff, wild card…
  - Map term to documents (events) like a hash map
    - "playoff" -> event 1, 2, 3
    - "swift" -> event 5, 6, n
  - Search "playoff" in description, return those events quickly
- Search by term on name, description, each field
- Geospatial queries supported
  - Speaker: uses a combination of quad trees and geohashing "if I'm not mistaken, don't quote me"
- Combine location + terms + dates in one query, using the various indexes

<a id="s7-3"></a>
### 7.3 Keeping Elasticsearch In Sync

- Not best practice as a primary data store
  - Durability concerns; no complex transaction support
  - Speaker's first startup used it as primary and "learned the hard way"
- Need changes in the primary DB propagated to Elasticsearch
- Option 1: application code dual-write
  - On event add, write to Postgres and to Elasticsearch
  - Complex logic: if one write fails, don't do the other; retry or reverse the first
  - Depends on product requirements; viable
- Option 2: **change data capture (CDC)**
  - Changes to the primary store go onto a stream
  - Consumed, and Elasticsearch is updated
  - In interviews often drawn as one arrow
    - Really a stream plus a worker doing the write
    - Clarify it's an abstraction
- Watch out
  - Elasticsearch has a writes-per-second limit (updates indexes on each write)
  - High-update systems need a queue, batching, etc.
  - Here: events, venues, performers rarely change or get added
    - At most tens, hundreds, maybe thousands a day: "absolutely nothing"
    - No queue needed; update on each change

<a id="s7-4"></a>
### 7.4 Caching Popular Searches

- "What if everybody searches for Taylor Swift?"
- Key observation: no ranking or personalization
  - Same query = same results; important for caching
- Option 1: **OpenSearch node query cache**
  - OpenSearch = AWS managed Elasticsearch
  - Speaker "believes" it's called that; "look that up"
  - Cache on each instance / shard; top 10K queries; LRU
  - Enable via config; quick, easy
- Option 2: Redis / Memcached
  - Key: search term (or normalized) to results
  - Must invalidate on updates
- Option 3: **CDN** (speaker's pick: quick, easy)
  - System likely already has a CDN for static images
  - Cache the API call and results for a short time (30 s to 1 min)
  - Same query from many users returns immediately, geographically close
  - Pros: super fast; great for very popular events
  - Cons
    - Less useful the more query permutations
    - Raw lat/long has too much precision: no overlap, no hits
    - A city like "San Francisco" might give enough hits
    - More params, fewer hits, wasted CDN space
    - If personalized recommendations are added, it no longer works
- Impressive to mention these if contextually relevant

<a id="s7-5"></a>
### 7.5 Surges: Real-Time Seat Map

- User opens an event: details + seat map (available vs booked)
  - Event CRUD service: event / venue / performer + tickets + cross-reference the lock
  - Locked tickets show as reserved / booked
- Problem
  - Accurate at load; stale after 1 s, 5 s, 5 min, 10 min
  - User clicks seats that look available but aren't; immediate error; bad UX
  - Happens a lot for popular events
- Make the map real-time: update the client when a ticket is reserved or booked
- Option 1: **long polling**
  - Client sends HTTP request; held open ~30 s to 1 min for the server to respond
  - Repeats in a loop
  - Super cheap, easy, no extra infrastructure
  - Perfect if users stay 1–5 minutes on the page
- Option 2: persistent connection, if users sit 5–30 min or hours
  - WebSockets: bidirectional, persistent
  - Instead: **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**
    - Persistent; server pushes whenever, while open
    - Key difference: SSE is unidirectional, server to client only
    - That's all we need: tell the client seats were taken
  - Setup: SSE between client, API gateway, Event CRUD service
    - Push every change to available / booked / reserved
  - Implementation more complex; probably out of scope

<a id="s7-6"></a>
### 7.6 Surges: Virtual Waiting Queue

- Problem with real-time map at Taylor Swift / Super Bowl / World Cup scale
  - Page loads, then within milliseconds all seats go black
  - 100K to 1M people fight for 10K to 100K seats
- Solution: a **choke point** that protects backend services and improves UX
  - **Virtual waiting queue**
- Enabled only for really popular events
  - Admin-enabled config
- Flow
  - Users enter the queue instead of the event page
  - Message: "thanks for your interest, you're in the queue, we'll let you know"
- Implementation
  - Could be Redis: cheap, lightweight
  - **Sorted set** as a priority queue by arrival time
  - Other implementations randomize for fairness
    - So users closest to servers don't always get in first
  - Event-driven: once 100 seats are booked, let the next 100 (or 1000) in
  - Pull users off the queue; maybe assign a token / session / user ID
  - Notify them, maybe over the same SSE connection
  - User enters and books
- "Simple but sophisticated"
  - The best answer isn't the most technically complex
  - It solves the problem simply, maybe creatively

<a id="s7-7"></a>
### 7.7 Strong Consistency (Already Covered)

- Covered in the HLD with the Redis lock

<a id="s7-8"></a>
### 7.8 Availability, Read-Heavy, General Scaling

- Speaker finds these the least interesting discussions
- What you'd say
  - AWS API Gateway is managed with its own load balancer
  - Each service has a load balancer and scales horizontally on memory / CPU
  - Databases: maybe sharding

<a id="s7-9"></a>
### 7.9 Aside: Estimation

- Speaker skipped back-of-envelope math after NFRs, on purpose, and recommends it
- Typical candidate: QPS, DAU, storage, "wow, it's a lot", keeps going
  - Interviewer learns nothing; design isn't informed
  - "Math without a purpose"
- Recommendation
  - Only calculate if the result directly influences the design
  - Usually in the HLD or deep dives
- Example: compute Postgres storage to decide whether to shard
  - If sharding: shard on **event ID** (most queries use it)
  - Or **venue ID** if shards are distributed geographically and users search nearby venues
  - No right or wrong; weigh pros and cons with the interviewer

<a id="s7-10"></a>
### 7.10 Caching Event Data

- Reads >> writes; event / venue / performer rarely change
  - "Cache them to hell"
- Redis cache: event ID -> event + venue + performer
- On DB update, invalidate or update the cache
- No eviction policy needed (LRU / LFU); probably all fit
  - Or bound it: e.g., last 4 months to next 2 years
- View API becomes "wicked fast"
  - Only the ticket query remains; it's dynamic, not cached

<a id="s8"></a>
## 8. Wrap-Up

- A solid design
  - Mid-level: passed "with flying colors"; overkill
  - Senior: definitely passes
  - Staff: probably, depending on execution and depth elsewhere
  - Principal: usually evaluated like staff
- To conclude
  - Look at the design: does it satisfy all FRs? All NFRs?
  - If yes to both, feel confident
- Invites comments on anything silly or a bad decision

<a id="s9"></a>
## 9. Final Board (Assembled From The Talk)

![Excalidraw board from the video](data:image/png;base64,)

- Image: the speaker's own Excalidraw board, exported as PNG and embedded in this file
- Text version below, assembled from the talk

```
Client
 ├─ CDN (search API cache, 30–60 s)
 └─ API Gateway (auth, rate limit, routing)
     ├─ Virtual Waiting Queue (Redis sorted set; popular events)
     ├─ Event CRUD Service ─▶ Redis (event/venue/performer cache)
     │      │  (SSE to client)  ─▶ Postgres
     │      └─ checks Ticket Lock (Redis, TTL 10 min)
     ├─ Search Service ─▶ Elasticsearch ◀─ CDC ◀─ Postgres
     └─ Booking Service ─▶ Ticket Lock, Postgres, Stripe (webhook back)
```

- NFRs at the end
  - Strong consistency for booking
  - High availability for search / view
  - Scalability for surges from popular events
  - Low-latency search (added during the design)
  - Read >> write
